bib.title: AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts

legacy_report:
SOURCE: AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts. Yanyu Yao, Shangze Li, Zhi Zheng, Hui Zheng, Qi Liu, Tong Xu, Enhong Chen (USTC, Anhui Univ.). arXiv:2606.19847v1 [cs.CL], 18 Jun 2026. Preprint; the text names no venue. Code: github.com/MINE-USTC/AtomMem.
COVERAGE: 67066 of 67066 chars read (main text, limitations, Tables 1-5, all appendices A.1-A.8, references). Figures 1-3 and 6-7 are plots or diagrams that I did not view. I read only their captions and the surrounding text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Distilling raw dialogue into atomic facts beats retrieval over the raw history, even with no hierarchy. The paper's own conclusion is "memory storage quality is paramount".
 number: Multi-hop F1 20.97 -> 37.03 (+76.6% relative); tokens 722k vs 827k. Single-hop J 57.07 -> 67.66. Temporal J 38.01 -> 59.50. Open-domain J 41.67 -> 52.08.
 setup: LoCoMo (avg >600 turns, 35 sessions), GPT-4o-mini backbone, top-k 10, all-minilm-L6-v2 embeddings, J judged by deepseek-v4-pro. AtomMem-Flat is facts only, with no events, profiles or graph.
 quote: "AtomMem-Flat significantly outperforms the standard LoCoMo baseline operating on raw dialogue history. For instance, on the challenging Multi-Hop reasoning tasks, it raises the F1 score from 20.97 to 37.03, yielding a 76.6% relative improvement."
 where: Sec 4.2, p.7; Table 1 and Table 2.
2. The full system beats the best prior memory systems on every category.
 number: J on multi-hop 68.44 vs 64.89 (LightMem); temporal 66.98 vs 51.09 (LightMem); open-domain 64.58 vs 54.17 (Mem0); single-hop 78.48 vs 78.00 (Mem0).
 setup: As claim 1. The authors re-implemented all baselines on GPT-4o-mini with matched top-k and embeddings. The single-hop lead is marginal.
 quote: "in Multi-Hop and Temporal tasks, AtomMem achieves substantial improvements over the strongest baseline, LightMem, increasing the J-score by 5.5% and 31.1%, respectively."
 where: Sec 4.2, p.7; Table 1.
3. Token cost is lower than Mem0 but not the lowest.
 number: AtomMem 21,357k tokens vs Mem0 55,300k (-61.4%); LightMem 5,022k; LoCoMo raw 827k; AtomMem-Flat 722k.
 setup: Total API tokens across the whole pipeline (construction plus answering) on LoCoMo. The Table 1 numbers show AtomMem at about 4x LightMem, whose J is lower.
 quote: "our system significantly reduces total token consumption by approximately 61.4% compared to the highly performant Mem0."
 where: Sec 4.2, p.7; Table 1.
4. Each added layer helps, with the effects below. Full results are in Table 2.
 number: Single-hop F1 56.66 full vs 50.91 without profile. Multi-hop J 68.44 full vs 62.76 without graph. Open-domain J 64.58 full vs 60.42 without graph.
 setup: LoCoMo ablation, GPT-4o-mini.
 quote: "Without this profile, the Single Hop F1 score drops from 56.66 to 50.91."
 where: Sec 4.3, p.8; Table 2.
5. Retrieving more memory helps up to a point, then hurts, even though recall keeps rising.
 number: Performance peaks around k=10 to 20 and drops above 20 (k swept 5-40). Seed count ks=10 is optimal; ks>10 degrades.
 setup: LoCoMo, k_f swept from 5 to 40. The paper states the setting it chose is k_f = 10.
 quote: "Despite continuous increases in Recall, system performance drops when k is greater than 20. This indicates that excessive irrelevant noise degrades the reasoning quality of the LLM."
 where: Sec 4.4, p.8; Fig 3; A.6.
6. It is cheap online but slow end to end. Retrieval itself is a small share of the latency.
 number: Total latency avg 3585 ms; retrieval pipeline 145.8 ms; graph rerank 109.9 ms; query-intent LLM call 2080 ms.
 setup: 1540 LoCoMo questions, run locally on an i7-10750H CPU.
 quote: "The entire retrieval process averages only 145.80 milliseconds."
 where: A.5, p.14-15; Table 3.
Secondary: LongMemEval (500 questions) was run for AtomMem only, with J of SSU 90.00, MS 67.67, TR 52.63, KU 79.49, SSA 76.79, SSP 80.00. This is Table 4, A.4, and there are no baselines.

MEMORY OPERATIONS (for the chapter)
- Extract: an SFT-tuned Qwen3-14B filters noise, resolves coreference, and anchors time. It was trained on 4,352 samples, with GPT-4o as teacher plus human refinement.
- Verify/dedupe: filter candidates by metadata, rank by hybrid similarity (0.7 embedding + 0.3 keyword Jaccard), then let an LLM store only the residual content and emit update tuples on conflict.
- Consolidate: facts are routed into LLM-summarised events.
- Profile: a session-end batch update that keeps versioned history H.
- Retrieve: three stages. Primary fact recall, then compensatory recall through the event layer, then associative recall by random walk with restart over entity, event and turn edges.
- The profile and fact layers never overwrite silently. Changes go through verification, and old profile states are archived.

BASELINES
- "LoCoMo" row in Table 1: this is "the standard LoCoMo baseline operating on raw dialogue history" (827k tokens). The paper does not say whether it is full-context or RAG over raw turns, and the Table 1 caption does not say either. Treat it as an unspecified raw-history baseline.
- There is no explicit no-memory baseline. There is no explicit full-context baseline: the paper never defines that setting. There is no separate simple-RAG baseline apart from the LoCoMo row.
- Compared systems: MemoryBank (Zhong 2023), A-MEM (Xu 2025), Mem0 (Chhikara 2025), MemoryOS (Kang 2025), LightMem (Fang 2026).
- The paper does not test whether memory helps versus a long-context model that sees everything.

LIMITS
- Authors concede three things: dependence on the base LLM's stability; text only (no images or audio); token efficiency "can be further optimized".
- Not shown: any no-memory or true full-context baseline. Only one backbone (GPT-4o-mini) is used. LoCoMo has about 10 conversations. LongMemEval has no baselines. There are no confidence intervals or seeds.
- J scores come from a single judge, deepseek-v4-pro. The judge prompt is explicitly generous: "you should be generous with your grading".
- The extractor is trained on LoCoMo-style synthetic dialogues from the LoCoMo generation pipeline. The paper claims no entity overlap with the test set, but the format is the same.
- Hyperparameters were tuned on LoCoMo, the same benchmark used for the headline result.
- Latency was measured on a CPU, with LLM calls dominating. Memory-construction cost is bundled into the token totals and not itemised.
- The ablation does not reproduce a clean ordering. In Table 2, "w/o Profile" and "w/o Graph" score above Flat on most metrics, which is expected. But Flat is not a strict prefix of the other ablations, because Flat drops events too.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- RAG: Lewis et al. 2020 (NeurIPS); REALM, Guu et al. 2020 (ICML); Self-RAG, Asai et al. 2024 (ICLR).
- Agent memory: Generative Agents, Park et al. 2023 (UIST); MemGPT, Packer et al. 2023 (preprint); MemoryBank, Zhong et al. 2023 (preprint); Think-in-Memory, Liu et al. 2023 (preprint); RET-LLM, Modarressi et al. 2023 (preprint); Mem0, Chhikara et al. 2025 (preprint, arXiv 2504.19413); A-MEM, Xu et al. 2025 (NeurIPS); MemoryOS, Kang et al. 2025 (EMNLP); RMM, Tan et al. 2025 (ACL); MEM1, Zhou et al. 2025 (preprint); LightMem, Fang et al. 2026 (ICLR).
- Benchmarks: LoCoMo, Maharana et al. 2024 (ACL); LongMemEval, Wu et al. 2025 (ICLR); PERMA, Liu et al. 2026 (preprint). Lost in the Middle, Liu et al. 2024 (TACL), is in the reference list.
- The random walk with restart / Personalized PageRank graph step comes from the PageRank family. The paper does not cite a source for it.

CODE: Fact-extraction prompt rules (Fig A.1, p.12): "Ignore 'noise'... Replace all pronouns... and temporal markers... with explicit entities and absolute dates... Rewrite in third person... If no high-value facts exist, output an empty fact list." Training sample (Fig A.2, p.13): "Emma got an A on her first psychology exam on the Friday before May 17, 2023." Hybrid score: Sh = a*sim_e + b*Jac(K). Default hyperparameters (Table 5, p.17): k_f=10, we=0.7, RWR eta=0.34.

FIGURES: Fig 2 (p.4), overall architecture: extractor -> facts -> events and profiles -> memory graph -> hierarchical retrieval. This is the one candidate for the chapter. Fig 1 (p.2) contrasts the flat or bloated storage of earlier systems with this design.

PROBLEMS: None in extraction. Table 1 columns run together in the text dump. I reconstructed them by position and checked the percentages against the table: 68.44/64.89 gives +5.5%, 66.98/51.09 gives +31.1%, and 21357/55300 gives -61.4%. The paper has no embedded instructions. "Realted Work" and the Fig numbering (Figures 4 and 5 captions for A.1 and A.2) are typos in the source.
